items.followUp: A 2 kg body moves at 6 m/s. Calculate its kinetic energy.

accept: energy possessed by a body due to its motion
rubric.why: Awards the mark for defining kinetic energy.
rubric.description: Defines kinetic energy as the energy a body possesses because of its motion.
rubric.how: State the defining relationship between kinetic energy and motion.

rubric.why: Work done on the body is the starting point of the derivation.
rubric.description: Uses work done, W = Fs.
rubric.how: Write the equation for work done by a force.

rubric.why: Connects the distance travelled to the final speed for a body starting from rest.
rubric.description: Uses the equation of motion with initial speed u = 0.
rubric.how: Write the resulting relation between v, a and s.

rubric.why: This is the required derived equation.
rubric.description: Derives and states the kinetic energy equation.
rubric.how: Substitute F = ma and s = v²/2a into W = Fs, giving KE = ½mv².

modelAnswer: Kinetic energy is the energy possessed by a body due to its motion.
The work done on a body starting from rest is W = Fs.
Using F = ma and v² = 2as, we have s = v²/(2a).
Therefore, KE = W = ma × v²/(2a) = ½mv².

items.followUp: A force of 60 N acts perpendicularly at a distance of 0.25 m from a pivot. Find the torque.

rubric.why: Recognises the force and lever arm given in the question.
rubric.description: Identifies the given force and distance.
rubric.how: Write F = 100 N and convert the distance to SI units.

rubric.why: Torque calculations require the distance in metres.
rubric.description: Converts the distance from centimetres to metres.
rubric.how: Show 10 cm = 0.10 m.

rubric.why: Uses the torque relation for a perpendicular force.
rubric.description: States the torque formula for a perpendicular force.
rubric.how: Write τ = Fd.

rubric.why: Shows the correct substitution of SI values.
rubric.description: Substitutes the force and perpendicular distance.
rubric.how: Write τ = 100 N × 0.10 m.

rubric.why: Awards the mark for the correct torque and unit.
rubric.description: Calculates the torque with the correct unit.
rubric.how: Evaluate the product and state the answer in N m.

modelAnswer: Given: F = 100 N, d = 10 cm = 0.10 m, and the force is perpendicular.
Formula: τ = Fd.
Substitution: τ = 100 N × 0.10 m.
Answer: τ = 10 N m.

items.followUp: A force of 50 N acts on an area of 2.0 cm². Calculate the pressure in pascals.

rubric.why: Identifies the force and contact area from the question.
rubric.description: Records the given force and contact area.
rubric.how: Write F = 75 N and A = 1.5 cm².

rubric.why: Converts the area to SI units before calculating pressure.
rubric.description: Converts the contact area into square metres.
rubric.how: Show 1.5 cm² = 1.5 × 10⁻⁴ m².

rubric.why: Uses the definition of pressure.
rubric.description: States the pressure formula.
rubric.how: Write P = F/A.

rubric.why: Shows correct substitution using the SI area.
rubric.description: Substitutes the given force and converted area.
rubric.how: Write P = 75 N/(1.5 × 10⁻⁴ m²).

rubric.why: Awards the mark for the correct pressure and unit.
rubric.description: Calculates pressure in pascals.
rubric.how: Evaluate the division and state the answer in Pa.

modelAnswer: Given: F = 75 N, A = 1.5 cm² = 1.5 × 10⁻⁴ m².
Formula: P = F/A.
Substitution: P = 75 N/(1.5 × 10⁻⁴ m²).
Answer: P = 5.0 × 10⁵ Pa.

items.followUp: What is zero error, and how does correcting it improve a measurement?

rubric.why: Identifies the instrument reading that must be checked before measurement.
rubric.description: States that an instrument may show a non-zero reading when the quantity being measured is zero.
rubric.how: Explain what the instrument reads when the true value is zero.

rubric.why: Explains why checking and correcting zero error matters.
rubric.description: States that correcting zero error removes an offset and improves measurement accuracy.
rubric.how: Explain the effect of the zero correction on the measured value.

modelAnswer: An instrument has zero error if it shows a non-zero reading when the quantity being measured is zero.
Checking and correcting zero error is essential to obtain accurate measurements and avoid systematic error.

items.followUp: Give one example each of a base unit and a derived unit.

rubric.why: Distinguishes base units by their independent, fundamental status.
rubric.description: States that base units are independent fundamental units.
rubric.how: Define base units or name suitable examples such as metre, kilogram or second.

rubric.why: Distinguishes derived units by how they are formed.
rubric.description: States that derived units are obtained by combining base units, with an example.
rubric.how: Define derived units or give an example such as m/s or newton.

modelAnswer: Base units are independent fundamental units, such as the metre, kilogram and second.
Derived units are formed by combining base units, such as m/s or the newton (kg m/s²).

items.followUp: Name the two methods used to add vectors and briefly describe each.

rubric.why: Recognises the graphical representation of a vector.
rubric.description: Names the graphical method or describes a vector as a directed line segment.
rubric.how: State that magnitude is shown by length and direction by the arrow.

rubric.why: Recognises the analytical or component representation of vectors.
rubric.description: Names the analytical/component method of representing vectors.
rubric.how: State that a vector can be expressed using components along coordinate axes.

modelAnswer: Graphical method: represent a vector by a directed line segment; its length shows magnitude and its arrow shows direction.
Analytical method: represent a vector by its components along chosen coordinate axes.

items.followUp: Define position and state the position of an object using a suitable reference point.

accept: location relative to a reference point
place relative to a reference point
rubric.why: A position must be specified relative to a reference point or origin.
rubric.description: Defines position as the location of an object relative to a reference point.
rubric.how: Include the idea of a reference point or origin in the definition.

rubric.why: Awards the mark for a clear example that specifies position relative to a reference.
rubric.description: Gives a suitable example of an object's position.
rubric.how: For example, state that a student is 5 m east of a pole.

modelAnswer: Position is the location of an object relative to a reference point.
For example, a student may be 5 m east of a pole.

items.followUp: State two ways to reduce friction between moving surfaces.

rubric.why: Lubricants reduce direct contact between surface irregularities.
rubric.description: Names lubrication as a method of reducing friction.
rubric.how: Give an example such as applying oil or grease.

rubric.why: Accepts another standard method that reduces friction.
rubric.description: Names another suitable method, such as using ball bearings or making surfaces smoother.
rubric.how: State one method other than lubrication.

modelAnswer: Lubricate the surfaces with oil or grease.
Use ball bearings or rollers to reduce friction.
